title: Present Perfect Continuous
subtitle: Emphasize the duration of an activity that started in the past and continues (or just stopped).
objectives: Form the present perfect continuous (have/has been + -ing)
Use it to emphasize how long an activity has been happening
Use it for an activity that has recently stopped, with visible results now

content.intro: This tense adds duration and "in-progress-ness" to the present perfect — it's less about the result and more about the activity itself, and how long it's been going on.

rules.heading: Form
rules.body: have/has been + verb-ing. I/you/we/they have been working. He/she/it has been working.

rules.heading: Use 1: duration up to now
rules.body:
• I have been studying English for three years. (started three years ago, still going)
  • She has been working here since 2020.

rules.heading: Use 2: recent activity, visible result
rules.body:
• You're out of breath — have you been running?
  • It has been raining — the streets are wet.

examples: I have been studying English for three years.
She has been working here since 2020.
It has been raining all morning.
They have been living in London for six months.
He looks tired — he has been working all day.

commonMistakes.wrong: I have been study English for three years.
commonMistakes.right: I have been studying English for three years.
commonMistakes.why: The continuous form needs the -ing verb, not the base form.

commonMistakes.wrong: I have been knowing her for years.
commonMistakes.right: I have known her for years.
commonMistakes.why: "Know" is a state verb (not an action) and doesn't normally take the continuous form — use the present perfect simple.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the present perfect continuous.

items.explanation: Third person singular: has + been + working.
A visible present result of a recent activity — present perfect continuous.

items.prompt: I ___ her for ten years. (a state, not an action)
items.explanation: "Know" is a state verb — use the present perfect simple, not the continuous.

items.incorrect: They have been live in London for six months.
answer: They have been living in London for six months.
items.explanation: The continuous form needs the -ing verb.

items.incorrect: She has being working all day.
answer: She has been working all day.
items.explanation: The correct participle after "has" is "been," not "being."

summary: Emphasizes duration (for/since) or a recent activity with a visible present result.
State verbs (know, like, believe, own) don't normally take the continuous form.
